name: Madagascar

facts.religion: Christian about 85%, traditional ancestor veneration widely practised

snapshot: Gen Z protests over water and power cuts brought down President Rajoelina in 2025, and an army colonel now runs a transition that promises elections.
culture: Madagascar's people descend from Austronesian sailors from Borneo and from East Africans, and Malagasy is related to languages of Indonesia. Famadihana, the "turning of the bones", sees families exhume ancestors, rewrap them in fresh cloth and dance with them. Hira gasy, all-day performances of song and oratory, are popular in the highlands.
society: About 90 percent of the island's plants and animals are found nowhere else, including lemurs, but deforestation has destroyed much of their habitat. Madagascar supplies most of the world's vanilla. It is one of the world's poorest countries, frequently hit by cyclones and drought, with the south suffering repeated famines.
situation: Madagascar is home to animals found nowhere else on Earth, and to one of its poorest populations: about three in four people live below the poverty line, and power and water cuts are routine in the capital. Its politics has swung between elections and coups since independence from France in 1960. In 2009 a young DJ-turned-mayor, Andry Rajoelina, took power with the backing of an elite army unit called CAPSAT. In October 2025 the same unit took power from him.

Youth-led "Gen Z" protests over water and electricity shortages began on 25 September 2025. On 11 October, CAPSAT commander Colonel Michael Randrianirina, who had been jailed in 2023 for allegedly plotting a coup, called on soldiers to refuse orders to fire on protesters. Rajoelina fled, parliament impeached him, and Randrianirina took power on 14 October, promising elections within 18 to 24 months (AFP via eNCA). The African Union suspended Madagascar. In 2026, the questions have been whether the colonel means it. He submitted a transition roadmap to the regional bloc SADC by its 28 February deadline, with presidential elections planned for 2027. Then on 9 March he abruptly sacked his prime minister, the businessman he had appointed in October, and the entire cabinet, without explanation (People Daily). Gen Z leaders who cheered the takeover say they want more say, and analysts describe protesters' "buyer's remorse" at a revolution they fear has been hijacked (ISS Africa). The record of Africa's other recent juntas, almost all of which missed their own election deadlines, does not encourage optimism.
power: A military-led transition. Randrianirina, confirmed as head of state by the High Constitutional Court, governs with a committee of army, gendarmerie and police officers and an appointed transitional government; parliament's role is limited.
